modalLead: A custom widget can be tried before it is saved: ask the address from the settings panel and see the answer that comes back, beside the figures your paths make of it. The presets now fill in the scheme an API key needs, a stored key can be looked at, and a speed reads in the units a connection is sold in.

items.text: Try a custom widget before saving it. The tile was the only place its answer was ever visible, and all a tile can say about a path that matched nothing is — four of those look the same whether the address is wrong, the key is wrong, or the JSON simply nests a level deeper than your boxes say. Config → Widgets → Settings now has a Try it block: Ask now makes the very request the widget describes and shows what came back, indented and in the service's own order, beside the figures your paths read out of it. Above both sit the facts — method, host, status, how long it took, how much arrived, and whether a sign-in went with it, which is the difference between a wrong key and no key at all. Asking saves nothing.

Keep watching, and see what moves. The same request every 5, 10, 30 or 60 seconds, with the figures that changed on the last beat marked for a moment — for a queue draining or a machine coming back up while you are looking at it. It asks nothing while the tab is in the background, and stops itself after five minutes rather than quietly polling somebody's service all afternoon.

GET or POST is a setting again. nextDash has always accepted both and the manual always said so, but the panel offered neither — the only way to give a widget POST was to edit its stored file by hand. It is a dropdown beside the address now. Nothing is sent with either: POST is for the services that answer a statistics endpoint on that method and no other.

See the key a widget has stored. A key typed into a custom widget goes into the credential file and never comes back, so the box over a saved one says Set — type to replace and nothing on screen can tell you what is actually in there. That matters most for an Authorization header missing its Bearer prefix: the service answers 401 exactly as it would to a wrong key. There is an eye beside the box now — press it to see what is stored, press it again to put it away.

Presets fill in the scheme an API key needs. Choosing Speedtest Tracker gave you the address, the paths and the header name, and a tile that answered 401 — because an Authorization value wants Bearer in front of the token and the box only asked for an “API key”. The presets now put the scheme in the box for you, ready for the token to go behind it. Not always Bearer: Paperless takes Token, Proxmox takes PVEAPIToken=, and each preset carries its own.

A speed reads as a speed. The new Speed format shows a figure in the units a connection is sold in — bits, in thousands — so a gigabit line reads 1.046 Gbps rather than 124.703 MB, which is the same measurement expressed so differently you cannot hold it against what your contract promised. It scales on its own, and carries three decimals so this week can be compared with last week. The Speedtest Tracker preset uses it.
